epithet: Amm al-Nabi (Uncle of the Prophet ﷺ)
summary: Al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib (RA) was the paternal uncle of the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ and one of the elder statesmen of Banu Hashim. He accepted Islam during or before the Conquest of Makkah and became a beloved Companion. His descendants, the Abbasids, went on to establish the Abbasid Caliphate, one of the most significant dynasties in Islamic history.
biography:
Al-Abbas ibn Abd al-Muttalib ibn Hashim al-Qurashi was born in Makkah around 568 CE, making him approximately two or three years older than his nephew, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ. He was the son of Abd al-Muttalib — the chief of Banu Hashim who had raised the Prophet as an orphan — and thus the Prophet's full paternal uncle. From early in his life, al-Abbas held a position of prestige in Makkah both as a member of the clan of Hashim and as the holder of the Siqayah — the hereditary custodianship of providing water from the Zamzam well to pilgrims during the Hajj season.

The precise date of al-Abbas's conversion to Islam has been a subject of scholarly discussion. The majority position, as recorded by al-Dhahabi in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' and Ibn Sa'd in al-Tabaqat al-Kubra, is that he embraced Islam privately while still in Makkah, before the Hijrah, but kept his Islam concealed for a time due to the complexities of his position among the Quraysh. The Prophet ﷺ used him as a confidential informant in Makkah, and al-Abbas sent letters to the Prophet ﷺ in Madinah alerting him to the Quraysh's military preparations — intelligence that proved vital. This correspondence is documented by Ibn Hisham in al-Seerah al-Nabawiyyah.

Despite this, al-Abbas was present on the opposing side at the Battle of Badr in 2 AH (624 CE), fighting with the Quraysh army. He was captured during the battle and held for ransom like the other prisoners. When the Muslims demanded ransom for him, the Prophet ﷺ did not exempt his uncle from this treatment, maintaining the principle of justice over family ties. Al-Abbas paid his ransom. Some scholars, including Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani in al-Isabah, note that al-Abbas later maintained his prior secret Islam was genuine, and his forced participation in Badr was under duress — a claim the Prophet ﷺ is reported to have acknowledged.

By the time of the Conquest of Makkah in 8 AH (630 CE), al-Abbas's Islam was public and complete. A well-known incident from the Conquest is that al-Abbas intercepted the leader of Makkah, Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, and brought him to accept Islam before the Muslim army entered the city — using al-Abbas's status as the Prophet's uncle to grant Abu Sufyan protection and safety. This act of strategic negotiation helped ensure the near-bloodless conquest of Makkah, which the Prophet ﷺ acknowledged. Ibn Hisham records the Prophet ﷺ saying: 'Abu al-Fadl [al-Abbas] has done well.'

After the Conquest of Makkah, al-Abbas participated in the Battle of Hunayn (8 AH), and this battle is where his loyalty and courage became most publicly evident. When a portion of the Muslim army fled in initial panic, al-Abbas — who had a powerful, resonant voice — stood beside the Prophet ﷺ and called out at the Prophet's instruction: 'O people of the Pledge of Ridwan! O people of Surah al-Baqarah!' This rallying cry brought the fleeing soldiers back to the Prophet's side, and the battle was won. Ibn Kathir in al-Bidayah wal-Nihayah describes this moment as one of al-Abbas's most consequential contributions to Islam.

Al-Abbas became one of the respected elders of Madinah following the Hijrah of the Muslim community. He transmitted hadith extensively, and his narrations are preserved in the major collections. The Prophet ﷺ honored him with great affection, often saying: 'Al-Abbas is my father's brother. Whoever harms al-Abbas harms me.' (recorded by al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah).

During the caliphates of Abu Bakr, Umar, and Uthman (RA), al-Abbas was a respected elder consulted on important matters. Umar ibn al-Khattab would seek his intercession (tawassul through his supplication) during times of drought, asking al-Abbas to make du'a to Allah — not to al-Abbas himself, but invoking his righteousness and his relation to the Prophet ﷺ. This incident is recorded in Sahih al-Bukhari and is often cited in scholarly discussions of the permissible forms of tawassul.

Al-Abbas died in Madinah in 32 AH (653 CE) at an advanced age, possibly 88 years old. He left behind a large family from multiple wives. His descendants through his son Abd Allah ibn al-Abbas (the great scholar Ibn Abbas) became founders of the Abbasid Caliphate, which ruled from Baghdad from 132 AH (750 CE) through 656 AH (1258 CE) — one of the longest and most influential dynasties in Islamic civilization.

key_events.event: Reportedly accepted Islam privately while maintaining outward neutrality in Makkah
Present at Battle of Badr on the Quraysh side; captured and ransomed
Participated in the Conquest of Makkah; brought Abu Sufyan to accept Islam
Rallied the fleeing army at the Battle of Hunayn with his resonant voice on the Prophet's instruction
Accompanied the Prophet ﷺ on the Tabuk expedition
Umar ibn al-Khattab sought his du'a as tawassul during drought in Madinah
Died in Madinah during the caliphate of Uthman ibn Affan; buried in al-Baqi'

notable_traits: Powerful, resonant voice — famously used to rally soldiers at Hunayn
Dignified elder statesman — commanded respect across tribal and political lines
Custodian of Zamzam — held the Siqayah, a position of great honor in Makkah
Deeply loyal to the Prophet ﷺ personally, demonstrating it under pressure at Hunayn
Father of the scholar Ibn Abbas and ancestor of the Abbasid dynasty
narrated_hadith_count: approximately 35 hadith in the major collections
